title: The Rookie
full_review:
Apple pie and baseball. You can't get more American than that, unless of course you're talking about second chances and making your dreams come true. Disney's latest film, "The Rookie," includes all of the above -- with the exception of the pie -- in an inspirational story that pulls on the heart strings as it nudges the audience to think about forgotten dreams that were somehow left by the wayside on the journey of life.

If the film weren't based on a true story, it might cause viewers to roll their eyes in disbelief. When Texas native Jim Morris (played by Dennis Quaid) first played professional baseball, he got as far as the Milwaukee Brewers' Class A team. But the twenty-something left-handed pitcher blew out his elbow and shoulder and had to retire. Ten years later, Morris, by this time 35 years old and what most would consider way past his prime, got another chance. The Tampa Bay Devil Rays signed the high-school chemistry teacher and baseball coach when he threw 98 mile per hour pitches during a tryout. A few months later, he came out of the bullpen at The Ballpark in Arlington, Texas in the Devil Rays' Major League uniform as the stadium crowd cheered madly for their hometown hero. He was the oldest rookie pitcher to play Major League baseball in 40 years.

By 35, with a wife and three kids, Morris (Quaid) was more concerned with teaching his students about the nucleus of a cell than throwing a fastball from the mound of a Major League baseball field. But then a funny thing happened. One day while offering the high school baseball team he coached a pep talk about never giving up, never quitting, the players threw the challenge back in his face. The Owls, on a wicked losing streak for the past several years, told him that if they made the state championships, Morris would have to try out for the Majors one more time. Needless to say, the Owls won the championship.

"The Rookie" is also a father and son story. Quaid is engaging as a father who comes to realize that following his dreams means setting a good example for his young son (Angus T. Jones) about developing one's God-given talents. Rachel Griffiths is Morris' reluctantly supportive wife, a strong Texas woman who holds down the fort while her hubby lives what at first she thinks is a pipe dream.

It is a rare film indeed that not only pleases and inspires but does so without discernible violence, sex or crude language. Director John Lee Hancock and writer Mike Rich have a simple, pleasing way of telling Morris' story. And what might be even more appealing to Catholic viewers is the presence to St. Rita -- patron saint of impossible dreams -- in the film. Whether Morris truly had a devotion to St. Rita or filmmakers took certain liberties to embellish Morris' story is almost beside the point. The positive recognition of a Catholic saint in a major motion picture is always welcome.

Now as charming as the film is, it does have some flaws. By the time Morris makes it to the Minor Leagues -- for the second time-- the story starts to sag a bit, becoming more mechanical than uplifting. Sometimes the movie plays like an after-school TV special. But it is so nice to see such a warm-hearted, stirring film on the big screen that this thought is only fleeting. By the end, viewers leave with the feeling that we've somehow shared in Morris' triumph.

You don't have to be a baseball fan to root for "The Rookie."

The U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-I -- general patronage. The Motion Picture Association of America has rated it PG -- parental guidance. (A-I) (PG)
(
2002
)
